package_info.package_manager: N/A (Java core/runtime, not a package manager)
package_info.package_versions: All Java versions supporting serialization (especially pre-patched JRE/JDK, vulnerable libraries like Apache Commons Collections, older Log4J, etc.)
package_info.why_malicious: The deserialization mechanism in Java can be abused to execute arbitrary code, load remote classes, or cause denial-of-service by manipulating serialized data streams. Attackers can craft malicious object streams (gadget chains) that exploit insecure deserialization logic, leading to remote code execution or system compromise.

execution_context.file_location: Serialized object stream (network/file input to ObjectInputStream)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Serialized javax.naming.Reference object with remote codebase URL
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At deserialization-time, the code leverages javax.naming.Reference to specify a remote codebase URL, causing the JVM to load and instantiate a class from a remote server, resulting in arbitrary code execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Loading and executing code from a remote location during deserialization is highly dangerous and enables remote code execution.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal deserialization should only reconstruct local, trusted objects. Loading remote code via Reference objects is unexpected and unsafe.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: JNDI is used for legitimate directory lookups in enterprise Java, but not for loading untrusted code during deserialization.
key_indicators: Presence of javax.naming.Reference in serialized stream

execution_context.file_location: Serialized object stream (network/file input to ObjectInputStream)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Gadget chain: ObjectInputStream.readObject() → AnnotationInvocationHandler.readObject() → Map(Proxy).entrySet() → ... → Runtime.getRuntime().exec()
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At deserialization-time, a crafted gadget chain triggers a sequence of method invocations, culminating in a call to Runtime.getRuntime().exec() with attacker-controlled arguments, resulting in arbitrary command execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Deserialization should not trigger arbitrary method calls or process execution. Chaining objects to reach Runtime.exec() is a hallmark of exploitation.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal deserialization reconstructs data, not executes code. Gadget chains abuse method invocation during deserialization.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: No legitimate use for such gadget chains in deserialization; method chaining is only for exploitation.
key_indicators: Use of known gadget classes (e.g., AnnotationInvocationHandler, LazyMap, InvokerTransformer)

execution_context.file_location: Serialized object stream (network/file input to ObjectInputStream)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Serialized array with field array length = INT_MAX (e.g., private int[] ids = new int[Integer.MAX_VALUE])
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At deserialization-time, the code attempts to allocate an array of size Integer.MAX_VALUE, causing the JVM to exhaust memory and crash, resulting in a denial-of-service.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Unusually large array allocations during deserialization are a classic denial-of-service vector.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal serialized arrays have reasonable lengths. INT_MAX-sized arrays are abnormal and dangerous.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: No legitimate use for such large arrays in typical business logic.
key_indicators: Array length set to Integer.MAX_VALUE or similar extreme values

attack_chain.action: Attacker crafts a malicious serialized object stream containing a Reference object or gadget chain.
Application deserializes the object stream using ObjectInputStream.readObject().
Malicious behaviors are executed: remote code is loaded (snippet_1), arbitrary commands are run (snippet_2), or system resources are exhausted (snippet_3).

behavioral_signatures: Presence of javax.naming.Reference or similar classes in serialized data
Unexpected method invocation chains during deserialization
Large or abnormal array allocations during deserialization
file_indicators: Serialized streams with gadget chain class signatures (e.g., AnnotationInvocationHandler, LazyMap, InvokerTransformer)
Serialized arrays with extremely large declared lengths
network_indicators: Outbound JNDI lookups to remote LDAP/RMI servers
Connections to attacker-controlled domains for class loading
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for deserialization of untrusted data, especially if the data contains references to javax.naming.Reference or known gadget classes. Flag serialized arrays with abnormally large lengths. Detect outbound JNDI lookups or remote class loading attempts during deserialization. Use static and dynamic analysis to identify code paths where deserialization is performed on untrusted input.
